account: Between 12 December 2018 and 29 March 2020 Google's deep-learning system graded fundus photographs in real time at nine primary-care sites of Thailand's national diabetic retinopathy screening program. On 27 April 2020 MIT Technology Review reported Google's own field study of the deployment in 11 clinics. Over a fifth of images were rejected. Nurses were frustrated by the rejections and by slow internet connections. When the system worked, it sped screening. On 7 March 2022 Ruamviboonsuk and colleagues reported the results of the deployment in The Lancet Digital Health. Google and Rajavithi Hospital funded their prospective interventional cohort study, and Google Health staff were among the co-authors. Of 7,940 patients screened, 7,651 were analyzed. Of these, 2,412 (31.5%) were referred for retinopathy, macular edema, ungradable images or low acuity. For vision-threatening retinopathy the system's accuracy was 94.7%, its sensitivity 91.4% and its specificity 95.4%. The retina specialists who over-read the images scored 93.5%, 84.8% and 95.5%. On 10 January 2025 Chotcomwongse and colleagues, two of them working for Google, reported that 89.1% of patients with a true-positive AI referral at a community hospital in Ayutthaya adhered to the referral. On 10 February 2025 The Nation Thailand reported that Google and Perceptra planned AI screening for about 1 million people in Thailand over a decade. It cited over 600,000 patients screened with the model globally. In a meta-analysis published on 17 April 2026, Oxford-led researchers reported that AI-assisted screening raised referral uptake, and they attributed much of the gain to redesigned care pathways. On 23 September 2026 Google and partner-site authors described in Nature Medicine how they scaled the same tool across India, Thailand and Australia. In October 2026 an AI Weekly alert reported that the model, ARDA, had screened more than one million patients, with Perceptra licensed to run screening in Thailand.

fields.account: Between 12 December 2018 and 29 March 2020 Google's deep-learning system graded fundus photographs in real time at nine primary-care sites of Thailand's national diabetic retinopathy screening program. On 27 April 2020 MIT Technology Review reported Google's own field study of the deployment in 11 clinics. Over a fifth of images were rejected. Nurses were frustrated by the rejections and by slow internet connections. When the system worked, it sped screening. On 7 March 2022 Ruamviboonsuk and colleagues reported the results of the deployment in The Lancet Digital Health. Google and Rajavithi Hospital funded their prospective interventional cohort study, and Google Health staff were among the co-authors. Of 7,940 patients screened, 7,651 were analyzed. Of these, 2,412 (31.5%) were referred for retinopathy, macular edema, ungradable images or low acuity. For vision-threatening retinopathy the system's accuracy was 94.7%, its sensitivity 91.4% and its specificity 95.4%. The retina specialists who over-read the images scored 93.5%, 84.8% and 95.5%. On 10 January 2025 Chotcomwongse and colleagues, two of them working for Google, reported that 89.1% of patients with a true-positive AI referral at a community hospital in Ayutthaya adhered to the referral. On 10 February 2025 The Nation Thailand reported that Google and Perceptra planned AI screening for about 1 million people in Thailand over a decade. It cited over 600,000 patients screened with the model globally. In a meta-analysis published on 17 April 2026, Oxford-led researchers reported that AI-assisted screening raised referral uptake, and they attributed much of the gain to redesigned care pathways. On 23 September 2026 Google and partner-site authors described in Nature Medicine how they scaled the same tool across India, Thailand and Australia. In October 2026 an AI Weekly alert reported that the model, ARDA, had screened more than one million patients, with Perceptra licensed to run screening in Thailand.
